User data types
text:
Mutually recursive variants
These require mutually recursive functions. Consider implementing a tree where each node can have a variable number of children.
type 'a tree =
  TreeLeaf of 'a
| TreeNode of 'a treeList 
and 'a treeList =
  Last of 'a tree
| More of 'a tree * 'a treeList;;
Now, say, to get the size, we can do
let rec treeSize t = match t with
  TreeLeaf x -> 1 |
  TreeNode x -> treeListSize x
and treeListSize l = match l with
  Last t -> treeSize t |
  More (t, r) -> treeSize t + treeListSize r;;
For example,
let t2 = TreeNode(More(
  TreeNode(More(TreeLeaf 1, More(TreeLeaf 2, Last(TreeLeaf 3)))),
  Last(TreeLeaf 4))) in
treeSize t2;;

title: 2027 CG:SHOP: multi-robot cover
text:
In the previous weeks, we’ve been focusing on the single-robot case, with either a square-cutter or circle-cutter. There is a very rich space in determining how to split the problem so that we can load-balance across multiple-robots. Namely, as in CG:SHOP 2027, we will consider the makespan objective: minimize the maximum length. In particular, our main tool will be an approximation algorithm for TreeCover: cover a graph using \(k\) trees minimizing the maximum size of any tree. See original paper: (Zheng et al. 2010).
problem formulation
The terrain consists of “large” cells, each binary (visitable or not), with each large cell a \(2 \times 2\) grid of small cells. Let \(n\) be the number of visitable small cells. There are many variations here that we can consider:

Weighted (large cells weight \(w_i \in \mathcal{Z}^{\ge 1}\)) or unweighted (large cells weight \(4\)) cases, where the cost of a move is the average of its start and end.
Robots are non-blocking (they can occupy the same cell); robots are sized as small cells.
Each robot is given an initial cell for each robot.
Without return (paths) or with return (tours).

And as typical, we consider the make-span objective (minimize the max length). Unsurprisingly, the problem is proven to be NP-hard, by reduction from 3-partition (split an array of length \(3m\) into \(m\) sets, all of equal weight and of size \(3\)) (Zheng et al. 2010).
See full notes.




References

Zheng, Xiaoming, Sven Koenig, David Kempe, and Sonal Jain. 2010. “Multirobot Forest Coverage for Weighted and Unweighted Terrain.” IEEE Transactions on Robotics 26 (6): 1018–31. https://doi.org/10.1109/TRO.2010.2072271.

title: 2027 CG:SHOP: lawn mowing with circles
text:
Now, we want to generalize lawn-mowing to shapes that are not necessarily a unit-square cutter. Remember that this unit-square cutter allowed us to reduce our problem to TSP, so that the order of visiting the grid exactly specifies the tour. For other shapes (namely, a circle), it is not as clear, and moreover, we would have no idea how to relate such a path to the optimal solution.
As such, we have two problems to tackle:
I want to briefly emphasize, once again, that this is hard!1 The optimal circle-cutter tour can do anything: not axis-aligned, and even the optimal tour has endpoints that are incredibly difficult to calculate (as discussed in (Fekete et al. 2023), roots of 16th-degree polynomials2). Compare to the case last week, where everything was integers, and it worked out much nicer.
key observation: Our avenue forward will be to consider local “patterns” of the unit-square tour, and figure out how to cover those patterns with the unit-circle. Then, we can lower-bound the optimal unit-circle tour by the optimal unit-square tour, which we already have tools to analyze (from last week, namely via the traveling salesman problem).

title: 2027 CG:SHOP: background
text:
Note: the following text is a mixture of what I said, what I think I said, and what I wish I said. As such, there may be small discrepancies from the lecture. Of course, there may be errors, and there is no peer-review.
This semester, we are preparing a submission for CG:SHOP (“CG:SHOP,” n.d.), part of the annual Symposium on Computational Geometry (SoCG). The problem for this year is multi-robot lawn mowing:

input: axis-aligned polygonal regions \(R\) (lawn) and \(\chi\) (cutter), and a parameter \(k\)
output: axis-aligned tours \(\tau_1, \ldots, \tau_k\) such that \(\bigcup_{i \in \mathopen{\unicode{x27E6}} k\mathclose{\unicode{x27E7}}} \bigcup_{p_j \in \tau_i} \chi(p_j) \supseteq R\), minimizing \(\max_{i \in \mathopen{\unicode{x27E6}} k\mathclose{\unicode{x27E7}}} \mathopen{}\mathclose{\left\vert \tau_i \right\vert}\)

Here, I am using the notation \(\mathopen{\unicode{x27E6}} k\mathclose{\unicode{x27E7}} = \left\{ 1, \ldots, k \right\}\), \(\chi(p)\) to denote placing the cutter centered at point \(p\). All regions are in the plane \(\mathcal{R}^2\). For this problem in particular, each edge of a region has integer side lengths, and so do the output tours (I will refer to this as integrality). See the 2nd meeting (www.cstheory.org/meetings/) for a slides/video description.
Now, this is a difficult problem to try and reason about. For example, some of the challenges include:

an infinite amount of potential tours and different regions; moreover without integrality, it is uncountable!
arbitrary regions \(R\) and \(\chi\) that can be non-convex or be any other nasty shapes
combinatorial explosion from planning \(k\) simultaneous tours

Therefore, for the first few weeks, we shall focus on some special cases which are a bit easier to think about. For example, we could:

only consider one robot at a time (avoiding the combinatorial explosion)
or restrict the shape of the cutter \(\chi\) or the region

or there are many other simplifications, as we will later see. For today (and next week), we will restrict \(\chi\) to be a unit square and consider only \(k=1\) (one robot).
See full notes.




References

“CG:SHOP: Computational Geometry: Solving Hard Optimization Problems.” n.d. Accessed October 23, 2026. https://cgshop.ibr.cs.tu-bs.de/.

title: Improving community detection with CVC, a new cluster ensemble method
text:
Abstract
Community detection is an unsupervised learning problem with many applications. In this study, we present Constrained Voting Consensus (CVC), a new ensemble clustering method that is designed to combine multiple clusterings, some of which may only cover a small portion of the network. We demonstrate that combining several dense subgraph clustering methods with standard methods within this ensemble approach produces a more accurate clustering than its constituent clustering methods. We also compare CVC to other ways of combining sets of clusterings, including the median consensus method, and show that CVC achieves higher accuracy and has better robustness. Furthermore, CVC can scale to very large networks with millions of vertices.

title: Using stochastic block models for community detection
text:
Abstract
A recent study reported by Park et al. (Improved community detection using stochastic block models, Springer, Heidelberg, 2025) in Complex Networks and their Applications 2024 showed that clusterings from three Stochastic Block Models (SBMs) in graph-tool, a popular software package, often had internally disconnected clusters when used on large real-world or synthetic networks. To address this issue, Park et al. (Improved community detection using stochastic block models, Springer, Heidelberg, 2025) presented a simple technique, Well-Connected Clusters (WCC), that repeatedly finds and removes small edge cuts of size at most \(\log_{10} n\) in clusters, where \(n\) is the number of nodes in the cluster, and showed that treatment of graph-tool SBM clusterings with WCC improves accuracy. Here we examine the question of cluster connectivity for clusterings computed using other SBM software or nested SBMs within graph-tool. Our study, using a wide range of real-world and synthetic networks ranging up to more than a million nodes, shows that all tested SBM clustering methods frequently produce communities that are disconnected, and that graph-tool improves on PySBM. We provide insight into why graph-tool degree-corrected SBM clustering produces disconnected clusters by examining the description length formula it uses, and explore the impact of modifications to the description length formula. Finally, we show that WCC generally provides an improvement in accuracy for both flat and nested SBMs, except for cases where nearly all nodes in the network are in very sparse ground-truth clusters. We also demonstrate that WCC scales to networks with millions of nodes.

title: 2026 July Mindbenders
text:
Combinatorics
There are \(6^6 = 46'656\) possible strings of 6 dice. We want to derive an expression for \(c_k\), the number of ways for there to be exactly \(k\) distinct numbers in that string.
We first pick the \(k\) distinct numbers, with there being \(\binom{6}{k}\) different ways of doing so. Then, we need to pick the histogram of counts for each of the \(k\) numbers. For \(c_4\), then this is
\[
  \binom{6}{4} \times \left(
    \frac{6!}{1! \cdot 1! \cdot 1! \cdot 3!} \times \frac{4!}{3! \cdot 1!} +
    \frac{6!}{1! \cdot 1! \cdot 2! \cdot 2!} \times \frac{4!}{2! \cdot 2!}
  \right) = 23'400
\]
And the answer is \(23'400 / 46'656 \approx 50.2\%\). For some reason, \(c_3 = c_5\); seems like a coincidence.
There are many other ways to do this combinatorially, e.g. with generating functions or inclusion-exclusion. These are besides the point here, but there are some more interesting approaches (many of which were in the pursuit of trying to find an intuitive reason for such a large probability mass)!

title: 2026 July Mindbenders
text:
Dynamic Programming
Another approach that is maybe less error prone is to do some dynamic programming. Let \(f(i, j)\) be the probability that we have \(i\) distinct numbers after \(j\) rolls. Then, we get the recurrence
\[
  f(i, j) =
  \begin{cases}
    1 & i = j = 1 \\
    0 & i > j \\
    \frac{i}{6} \times f(i, j-1) + \frac{6-i}{6} f(i - 1, j) & \text{otherwise}
  \end{cases}
\]
i.e. we sum up the cases where after a new roll, we get a distinct or not.



Summing up each column gives a probability of exactly \(1\). This also gives us a simpler closed form, namely, we just sum up all the paths! Indeed,
\[
f(i, j) = \left( \prod_{k=7-i}^{5} \frac{k}{6} \right)
          \times
          \left( \sum_{1 \le k_1 \le \ldots \le k_{j - i} \le i} \frac{ k_1 \cdot \ldots \cdot k_{j-i} }{6^{j-i}} \right)
\]
Calculating \(f(4, 6)\), the probability of getting \(4\) distinct numbers after \(6\) rolls, we have
\[
  f(4, 6) = \frac{3}{6} \frac{4}{6} \frac{5}{6} \times \sum_{k_1=1}^4 \sum_{k_2=k_1}^4 \frac{k_1 \cdot k_2}{6^2}
\]

title: 2026 July Mindbenders
text:
Hitting Times
Let us consider aa related problem: how many trials does it take until we get \(k\) distinct rolls. The number of rolls until we get our first distinct follows \(\text{Geometric}(p = 1)\). Our second distinct element follows \(\text{Geometric}(p = 1 - 1/6)\). In general, to get the \(k\) -th distinct, it follows \(G_k = \text{Geometric}(p_k = \frac{7 - k}{6})\). The expected number of rolls to get \(k = 1, \ldots, 6\) distinct elements are thus:
\[
  1, 2.2, 3.7, 5.7, 8.7, 14.7
\]
But, if we recall from our introductory statistics classes, this feels a lot like the Poisson and Gamma duality. The probability of counting \(\ge 4\) successes in \(6\) rolls is the same as it taking \(\le 6\) rolls to get the \(4\) -th success.
We can proceed in a similar path, deriving an analogous for the Gamma distribution. In particular, let \(T_k = G_1 + \ldots + G_k\) be the rolls until we get the \(k\) -th distinct element. Then, we want to calculate
\[
  \textbf{Pr}(T_4 \le 6) - \textbf{Pr}( T_5 \le 6 )
\]
The full calculation is a bit annoying, and I have instead attached it. In short, probability generating functions are useful.

title: 2026 July Mindbenders
text:
Embeddings
An extremely powerful tool in stochastic processes, which I hope to learn more about, is to embed this discrete chain into some more general process. Finally, we restrict our view of that more general process to the events that we care about.
This in general is known as Poissonification, and I first saw the idea with context of hashing in a UIUC theory seminar. We suppose we throw \(m = \textbf{Poisson}(\lambda)\) die, and then condition on the event that \(m = 6\). The really elegant result from this is that we avoid the negative correlation of the occupancy indicators \(X_i\). In particular, if we look instead at the Multinomial distribution of the counts of each dice, then
\[
\begin{align*}
  & \textbf{Pr}(\textbf{Multinomial}(m, (p_1, \ldots, p_6) = (n_1, \ldots, n_6); m \sim \textbf{Poisson}(\lambda)) \\
  & = e^{- \lambda} \frac{\lambda^m}{m!} \times \frac{m!}{\prod_{i=1}^6 n_i!} \prod_{i=1}^6 p_i^{n_i} = \prod_{i=1}^6 e^{- \lambda p_i} \frac{(\lambda p_i)^{n_i}}{n_i!}
\end{align*}
\]
where we recognize each individual term in the product as the mass function for \(\textbf{Poisson}( \lambda p_i )\). We not only avoid the negative correlation, but we get pure independence! At this point, by conditioning on \(m\), we can do the calculation and get an answer.
In fact, if one remembers the construction of a Poisson process, then it should be clear why Possionification leads to this nice independence property. Suppose we set a timer \(T \sim \textbf{Exponential}(\lambda / 6)\) independently for each of the \(6\) bins. Then, a dice is rolled whenever a timer is fired, and the timer gets reset.
Here, the waiting time between rolls of the dice follow the minimum of \(6\) independent \(\textbf{Exponential}(\lambda / 6)\) timers, i.e. the gap between each of the each of the dice rolls follows \(\textbf{Exponential}(\lambda)\). Thus, by the construction of Poisson process, then the number of dice rolls at a given time \(t\) follows \(\textbf{Poisson}( \lambda t )\). Moreover, because exponential random variables are memoryless, then the increment between a dice rolling in each bin follows \(\textbf{Exponential}(\lambda / 6)\), and again by construction of Poisson, then the number of balls in a given bin follows \(\textbf{Poisson}(\lambda t / 6)\).

title: 2026 January Momath Mindbender
text:
Puzzle from here. Consider a ladybug starting on the 12-hand of the clock. During each timestep, it will choose to walk either counterclockwise or clockwise, each with 50% probability. What is the probability that the last new number it visits is 6?
It will be useful to establish consistent notation. Let \(p_y\) be the probability that \(y\) is the last new number the ladybug visits. Let \(X_t\) be the position of the ladybug. Let \(T_y\) be the first time where \(X_t = y\).
I will also use \(P_x( ... )\) to denote the probability of an event given the starting point of a random walk of \(x\).

Gamblers Ruin
The first solution I came up with relies on the setup called “Gambler’s Ruin”. Consider a 1-D symmetric random walk starting at \(0 < x < d\). I claim that \(P_x(T_d < T_0) = \frac{x}{d}\).
First, observe that \(E(X_t) = x\) (this is called a Martingale process). This is because at each time step, we make no expected progress towards either endpoint. Therefore, at time \(T = \min( T_d, T_0)\), then we obtain the equation
\[
  x = E(X_0) = E(X_T) = 0 P(X_T = 0) + d P(X_T = d) = d P(T_d < T_0)
\]
which proves our claim.


Solution One
Now, to solve the puzzle, it remains to enumerate some simple cases. Consider the sequence in which the ladybug sees new numbers. Then, in order for 6 to be last, then it must either see 5 before 7 before 6, or 7 before 5 before 6. That is,
\[
  p_6 = P_{12}(T_5 < T_7 < T_6) + P_{12}(T_7 < T_5 < T_6)
\]
We can decompose
\[
  P_{12}(T_5 < T_7 < T_6) = P_{12}(T_5 < T_7) \cdot P_5(T_7 < T_6)
\]
and
\[
  P_{12}(T_7 < T_5 < T_6) = P_{12}(T_7 < T_5) \cdot P_7(T_5 < T_6)
\]
so that plugging in our expression
\[
  p_6 = (1/2) \cdot (1/11) + (1/2) \cdot (1/11) = 1/11
\]


Solution Two
Following this, I immediately noticed that \(p_1 = p_2 = \ldots = p_{11} = 1/11\). All the probabilities are uniform! This hints that there is a simpler explanation.
Indeed, in order for 6 to be the last new number visited, there must be an arc between 5 to 7, or from 7 to 5. All the steps before reaching either 5 or 7 are superfluous. Therefore, \(p_x = P_5(T_7 < T_6)\).
In words, the probability of seeing 6 last is the probability of starting to one side of 6 and reaching the other side of 6 without hitting 6. This holds for any starting position.
Now, as there are 11 probabilities, the final step is to show that they sum to 1. One way of doing this (although there are likely many) is to shift a perspective: instead of varying the starting point, vary the end point. As there must be some number that is the last one visited, those probabilities must add to 1.

Consider an infinitely long sequence of coin flips, i.e. with \(p\) probability heads and \(1-p\) probability tails. You get points for non-overlapping pairs of consecutive heads. Notation
Let us introduce some notation. - \(X_m\), the state of the markov chain after \(m\) steps - \(P^m(x,y)\) be the probability of moving from state \(x\) to \(y\) in exactly \(m\) steps. - \(N_n(x,y) = \sum_{m=1}^n 1_{y}(X_m)\), the number of visits to state \(y\) in \(n\) steps, starting at state \(x\). - \(G_n(x,y) = E(N_n(x,y)) = \sum_{m=1}^n P^m(x,y)\), the expected number of visits to \(y\) from \(x\) in \(n\) steps. - \(T_{x,y}^r = \min \{ n \ge 1 \mid N_n(x,y) \ge r \}\), the earliest time to hit \(y\) exactly \(r\) times - \(m_{x,y} = E(T_{x,y}^1)\), the expected time to hit \(y\) starting at state \(x\), i.e. the hitting time
For brevity, \(m_y = m_{y,y}, T_y = T_{y,y},\)…

title: Cycle Analysis
text:
Hitting Times and Stationary Distribution
Recall we want to find \(\pi_y\), the stationary distribution of the markov chain.
Theorem: The stationary distribution is the reciprocal of the hitting time.
\[
\pi_y = \frac{1}{m_y} = \lim_{n \to \infty} \frac{N_n(y)}{n}
\]
proof: First, we show the second equality, that the ratio \(N_n(y, y) / n\) approaches \(1/m_{y}\). For \(i \ge 1\), we consider \(\omega^i = T_{y}^i - T_{y}^{i-1}\), the marginal time to cycle back to \(y\) for the \(i\)-th time. Since our transitions are memoryless, then \(\omega^i\) are iid. Now, by the law of large numbers,
\[
\frac{T_{y}^k}{k} = \frac{1}{k} \sum_{i=1}^k \omega^i \to E(\omega) = m_{y}
\]
Finally,
\[
\frac{T_{y}^{N_n(y)}}{N_n(y)} \le \frac{n}{N_n(y)} \le \frac{T_y^{N_n(y) + 1}}{N_n(y) + 1}
\]
where the left and right both converge to \(m_y\). Thus, \(\frac{n}{N_n(y)}\), and moreover \(\frac{n}{G_n(y)}\), both converge to \(m_y\) as well.
Now, for the first equality, note that for any \(m\), \(\pi_y = \sum_{x \in S} \pi(x) P^{m}(x,y)\). Therefore, when we sum over \(m\), we have
\[
\pi_y = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{m=1}^n \sum_{x \in S} \pi(x) P^m(x,y) = \sum_{x \in S} \pi(x) \frac{G_n(x,y)}{n}
\]
Moreover, this holds as \(n \to \infty\), so recalling that \(\sum_x \pi(x) = 1\), then we find that
\[
  \pi_y = \lim_{n \to \infty} \sum_{x \in S} \frac{G_n(x,y)}{n} \pi(x) = \sum_{x \in S} \pi(x) \frac{1}{m_y} = \frac{1}{m_y}
\]
Thus concludes the proof.

title: Cycle Analysis
text:
Computing Hitting Times using Cycles
The hitting time \(m_y\) is the expected number of steps starting at \(y\) before reaching \(y\) again. We can compute this by enumerating all (possibly countable infinite) cycles, computing the probability of taking it, and find the expected length.
I illustrate this by example. Consider the following two state Markov chain with states \(T\) and \(H\). Let \(P(T, H) = p\), \(P(H, T) = q\), and self loops \(1-p\) and \(1-q\) respectively.



To find the hitting time (and therefore, the stationary distribution) \(m_T\), then we have the following cycles: \(e_4\), \(e_1 e_3\), \(e_1 e_2 e_3\), \(e_1 e_2 e_2 e_3\), …
Therefore, we can find the average cycle length, i.e. the hitting time, as
\[
\begin{aligned}
m_T & = p(e_4) \cdot 1 + p(e_1 e_3) \cdot 2 + p(e_1 e_2 e_3) \cdot 3 + p(e_1 e_2 e_2 e_3) \cdot 4 + \ldots \\
    & = (1-p) + \sum_{\ell=0}^\infty (\ell + 2) pq (1-q)^\ell \\
    & = (1-p) + 2pq + p(1-q) \sum_{\ell = 0}^\infty (\ell + 2) q(1-q)^{\ell - 1} \\
    & = (1-p) + 2pq + p(1-q) (2 + 1/q) = \frac{p + q}{q}
\end{aligned}
\]
Thus, \(\pi_T = \frac{p}{p+q}\).
We can now find \(\pi_H\) in one of several ways. First, \(\pi_H + \pi_T = 1\), so that \(\pi_H = \frac{p}{p+q}\).
Alternatively, we can note that \(\pi_H / \pi_T\) is the averaged number of times we visit \(H\) in the above cycles. That is,
\[
\begin{aligned}
\frac{\pi_H}{\pi_T} & = p(e_4) \cdot 0 + p(e_1 e_3) \cdot 1 + p(e_1 e_2 e_3) \cdot 2 + \ldots \\
                & = \sum_{\ell=0}^\infty (\ell + 1) pq (1-q)^\ell \\
                & = pq + p(1-q) \sum_{\ell = 0}^\infty (\ell + 1) q(1-q)^{\ell - 1} \\
                & = pq + p(1-q) (1 + 1/q) = \frac{p}{q}
\end{aligned}
\]
so that indeed, \(\pi_H = \frac{p}{q} \frac{q}{p+q} = \frac{p}{p+q}\).
We can summarize this procedure into the following theorem:
Theorem: Let \(x\) be any state in a finite irreducible Markov chain, and \(C_x\) be all cycles from \(x\). Then, for any state \(y\),
\[
\pi_y = \frac{ \text{average visits to } y \text{ in } C_x }{ \text{average length of } C_x }
\]
Note that here, we say cycles to allow repeated links, but passing through the start state exactly once.
proof: We partition the walk into stages, where each stage is delimited by a cycle in \(C_x\). Then, \(N_n(y)\) is sum of visits to \(y\) in the \(k\)-th stage.
\[
\frac{N_n(y)}{n} = \frac{N_n(y)}{G_n(x) m_x} = \frac{1}{m_x} \frac{N_n(x)}{G_n(x)} \frac{1}{N_n(x)} \sum_{k=1}^{N_n(x)} ( \text{visits to } y \text{ in } k \text{-th cycle} )
\]
Now, \(\frac{N_n(x)}{G_n(x)} \to 1\), and \(\frac{1}{N_n(x)} \sum_{k=1}^{N_n(x)} (..)\) approaches the average visits to \(y\) in \(C_x\). Moreover, the LHS approaches \(\pi_y\), and \(m_x\) is the average length of \(C_x\).
Thus, taking limits, indeed
\[
\pi_y = \frac{ \text{average visits to } y \text{ in } C_x }{ \text{average length of } C_x }
\]

title: 2026 February and March Mindbender
text:
Puzzle Statement
Consider an integer 2-D grid. A bacterium begins at the origin. Each bacteria may divide; that is, a bacterium at the point \((x, y)\) can be replaced by one at \((x+1, y)\) and \((x, y+1)\), supposing those two squares were previously bacteria-free. Roughly, how many divisions must take place before the closed box with corners at \((0,0), (0,3), (3,3)\), and \((3,0)\) is clear of bacteria?

\[
f(w, h) =
\begin{cases}
  1 & w = h = 1 \\

title: 2026 February and March Mindbender
text:
Simulations
Ok, at this point I gave up and wrote a simple simulation to see how long it would take. In a loop, I would: - check if there are any bacteria in the \(w \times h\) grid - try to get that bacteria to divide - if there was a bacteria in the way, then recurse to split that other bacteria
So I wrote this up and ran it. Then waited. Then waited. Then waited…
At this point, I got suspicious. Looking through the states, it seemed that I entered an infinite recursive descent.

title: 2026 February and March Mindbender
text:
The Solution
Finally, it got through in my head that it may not be possible to clear the grid. How would I prove this?
I recalled a similar problem my friend showed me. Similar, there was an integer grid of bacteria, but now there were infinite bacteria at every coordinate \((x, y)\) for \(x \le 0\). They divide in a peculiar way, with two (orthogonally) adjacent bacteria mating to spawn a new bacteria. That is, there are two ways they can divide: - a bacteria at \((x, y)\) and \((x+1, y)\) being replaced with \((x+2, y)\) - a bacteria at \((x, y)\) and \((x, y+1)\) being replaced with \((x, y+2)\) The question is can a bacteria reach \(x=5\)?
A general approach towards solving such problems is to find invariants. Suppose each configuration of bacteria has some potential that is maintained by these divisions. I’ll leave the solution to this related problem hidden, but as a hint, the golden ratio shows up!
Suppose we assign a value to each grid \((x, y)\), so that \(\varphi(x,y) = 2^{-(x+y)}\). The potential is the sum of \(\varphi\) over occupied grid positions. With this, upon a split,
\[
\varphi(x,y) = \varphi(x+1, y) + \varphi(x,y+1)
\]
so that the potential is constant! The starting potential is \(1\). What must be the potential be if the \(4 \times 4\) grid was empty? Well, there can be at most one bacteria on each grid square, so
\[
\begin{aligned}
  \varphi& \le \sum_{x, y \ge 0} \varphi(x, y) - \sum_{0 \le x, y \le 3} \varphi(x, y) \\
       & = \sum_{x=0}^\infty 2^{-x} \sum_{y=0}^\infty 2^{-y} - \frac{225}{64} \\
       & = 2 \sum_{x=0}^\infty 2^{-x}  - \frac{225}{64} = 4 - \frac{225}{64} = \frac{31}{64} < 1
\end{aligned}
\]
So the potential must decrease! However, divisions do not change the potential, so it is impossible to clear the grid.
Note that even clearing a \(3 \times 3\) grid is impossible, as the remaining potential adds up to \(\frac{30}{32} < 1\).

title: 2026 February and March Mindbender
text:
Pigeonhole and Solution
Unfortunately, I have seen this puzzle before as an application of the pigeonhole principle.
The first observation to make is that the disjointness only means that you need to choose two distinct subsets. That is, given two overlapping but distinct subsets that add to the same sum, then removing the overlapping numbers would find a winning pair of disjoint subsets.
Given 10 numbers \(x_1, \ldots, x_10\), there are \(2^{10} - 2 = 1022\) possible subsets (ignoring trivial ones). However, any subset must sum to at least \(1+2+\ldots+10 = 55\), and at most \(100+99+\ldots+91 = 955\), so there are \(901\) possible sums. As \(1022\) subsets must have a range of \(901\) values, two of them must have the same sum, by pigeonhole!
Pick those two subsets, remove the overlapping values, and thus you can always find two disjoint non-empty subsets of the same value!

title: 2026 Sept/Oct Mindbenders
text:
It has been too long since my last post, so let’s get back into it with some easy. Given two random balls that intersect in \(\mathbb{R}^d\); what is the expected volume of their intersection?
Of course, the above is actually underspecified (see Bertrands paradox). More precisely, we specify that we have a ball at the origin, and a second ball sampled uniformly with center inside the ball of radius \(2\).


Somehow, I managed to overcomplicate this quite a bit. So first, consider \(d=1\). By symmetry, we can assume WLOG that the random ball always has positive center. Thus, an integral obtains the answer
\[
  \int_{0}^1 (0.5) (2-x) \text{d}x + \int_1^2 (0.5) (x - 1) \text{d}x = 1
\]
where \((2-x)\) and \((x-1)\) are the lengths of intersection between two intervals of length \(2\), for \(x\) center less than 1 or between 1 and 2 respectively, and \(0.5\) is the probability density at any point.
A slightly nicer, but equivalent integral, is to consider the left endpoint from \(-1\) to \(1\), so that the area of intersection is always \(1-x\):
\[
  \int_{-1}^1 (0.5) (1-x) \text{d}x = 1
\]
This approach does not extend to 2D easily (lots of gross algebra). Somehow, I thought there were a few things that should make this nice:

we have two objects that are the same shape
the particular object is a sphere, which is nicely symmetric

I wanted to use both of these properties, and so what I thought was to consider a random process with both of these intervals. Originally, I wanted them to have centers anywhere in the plane, but then the density functions are hard to define. Thus, I tried having them be contained in some region \(A(r)\), where \(r\) is some scaling factor that I will have limit towards \(\infty\).
I remembered that the expected distance between two points in a rectangle in \(\mathbb{R}^d\) can be calculated (which is relevant in k-nearest neighbors, with the curse of dimensionality)> Thus, intuitively, I thought that this meant we can calculate the probability of them intersecting, and use the decomposition
\[
\begin{align}
  \textbf{Ev}(\text{area of union}) & = \textbf{Ev}(\text{area of union} \mid \text{intersect}) \textbf{P}(\text{intersect}) \\
                                    & + \textbf{Ev}(\text{area of union} \mid \text{not intersect}) \textbf{P}(\text{not intersect})
\end{align}
\]
Now, given that two balls don’t intersect, the area of union is easy (just the sum). The area of union given they intersect is what we want to find. So, what remains is to find the probability of not intersecting (which is perhaps a simpler integral, of which I doing in the past), and also the area of the union. Then, this area of union can be calculated using linearity of expectation; as each ball is placed independently, if \(p\) is the probability that a point is not covered by one ball, then \(p^2\) is the probability that it is not covered by both.
Doing this calculation… is messy and I started realizing there is probably some better way. Indeed, because I am already using linearity of expectation, looking at the probability of each point, it is actually easy to calculate it directly!



Consider again the process where we place a unit disk with center uniformly chosen from the disk of radius \(2\). We know any point \(p\) in the intersection (with this random disk, and the disk at the origin) is within the disk of radius \(1\) from the origin. Then, for this point, we can consider the probability that its in the intersection, and then sum up over all points in the unit ball.
Now, consider where must the second ball be in order for \(p\) to be in the intersection – the center must be in the unit ball centered at \(p\)! The probability that this is the case is exactly \(2^{-d}\), as this is the ratio of the volume of a unit ball (the success space) over the volume of a ball of radius \(2\) (the sample space). Putting this together, we obtain an answer of
\[
  \frac{\pi^{d/2}}{\Gamma(d/2 + 1) \cdot 2^d}
\]
which comes from the volume of a unit ball embedded in \(\mathbb{R}^d\).
I tried to exploit too much structure in the problem, before trying more straightforward methods. Think about what is relevant; work out some examples!

title: 2026 Sept/Oct Mindbenders
text:
September
Given a 10-digit number, ending in an odd number excluding \(5\), show that there is a multiple that consists only of ones.
I have no idea what p-adic numbers are, but I’ve seen visuals that remind me of this. In any case, the following documents my stream-of-thoughts for solving this puzzle.

attempts
Taking my lesson from October, I considered some examples. First, I wondered if the \(10\)-digit in the problem was significant, so I tried some fewer-digit numbers. For \(3\), then \(111\) is a multiple.
For \(7\), then it was not obvious how to find a multiple with all ones. Suppose there is a multiple, say \(y\). But we know that the first digit of \(y\) must be a \(3\). Then, \(3 \times 7 = 21\), and we actually know the next digit of \(y\) must be a \(7\) (so that the second digit of \(yx\) is a \(1\)). Then, \(73 \times 7 = 511\), and the next digit must be an \(8\) (so the \(3\)rd digit of \(yx\) is a \(1\)). Repeating this, we find \(15873 \times 7 = 111111\).
Actually, we are building up each digit of \(y\) step by step. And each digit of \(y\) is forced to be what we say it is (note that it is not unique, as this process can be continued step by step). Thus, we have an algorithm for finding it, if it exists, we just have to characterize if it can ever fail, or ever fail to terminate.
Now, to prove an algorithm terminates, usually we can find some sort of potential function that is bounded, and goes down at some rate. Of course, finding these is not typically quite difficult.
So, what could go wrong with the algorithm? Let’s give some more notation here. Let \(z_k\) be the first \(k\) digits of \(z\) (starting from least significant), which we are building up incrementally. If the first non-one digit of \((xy)\) is strictly less than \(k\), then we’re screwed (since adding more digits can never change a digit before \(k\)). We’re safe in this regard; inductively, we start from \(k=0\), and at each step of adding another digit to \(y\), we create at least one more \(1\) of \((xy)_k\).
Thus, we won’t ever get into a failing state. But it is still hard to argue that this process terminates.
One idea I had is to consider the most significant non-one digits (as they’re the only real signal from our process), and argue that number always decreases in some metric. This number definitely does not always decrease (e.g. for \(x = 7\), then we go from \(2\) to \(5\) to \(6\) to \(4\) to \(1\), after which we terminate). It seems to have the never increase the number of digits, and this is actually easy to show: if \(z\) is this number, then \(cz\) for \(c < 10\) has at most one more digit than \(z\), and since the last digit is trimmed off in the process, we found a non-increasing. We have the first thing we need: something that is bounded.
All that’s left is to argue that we can never visit the same number twice, and we win. Suppose we do visit the same number twice, then let \(y_1\) be when we first visit it, and \(y_2 \circ y_1\) the second time (where \(\circ\) denotes string concat). Writing this equationally, we have \((y_2 \circ y_1) \times x = (y_1 \times x) \circ (1 \circ \ldots \circ 1)\), but this actually means that \(y_2\) is all ones. Moreover, as its a circle, adding another repetition of \(y_2\) would also return back to the same potential. This means that our greedy algorithm will continually pick \(1\), which is absurd.
We are done! We have constructed a greedy algorithm that for any positive odd number \(x\) not divisible by \(5\), will find a multiple that is all ones. To do this, it incrementally builds the factor digit by digit. At each step of the algorithm, the number of non-one digits never increases, and also the number formed by the non-one digits is always distinct, and so this process terminates.

title: Improved Methods for \(k\)-Core Community Search
text:
Abstract
Community search based on user-specified query nodes is complementary to community finding or graph clustering. Prior work in community search is divided into optimizing for external separateness or internal cohesiveness, which does not scale well networks of over a billion edges. We present SteinerKCore, a new scalable k-core based community search algorithm for multi-vertex queries. We also present Par-ShellStruct, a parallel algorithm for building the ShellStruct data structure used for k-core community search. We show that our implementations in Icebug, an open-source toolkit for large-scale network analysis, are both more efficient and more scalable than comparative tools, being able to perform on a benchmark network of 273M and 5.1B edges using just 64GB RAM and under 4 hours runtime with 16 CPUs.

title: Modeling citations and cartels
text:
Abstract
Citation data are widely used to inform researchers and administrators. Interpreting the results of citation analysis is non-trivial on account of uncertainty around motivations for citation, varied disciplinary practices, data quality, standards for quality, and the lack of ground truths. In-silico approaches that harness autonomous behavior and randomness offer an option in this regard. We have developed an agent-based model of citation that allows us to parsimoniously model citation dynamics at article and author levels. We characterize the model through baseline simulations, sensitivity, and ablation analysis. We also model the behavior of cartels that seek to manipulate citations. We observe an early advantage to cartels that is lost over time implying that, on balance, cartel membership may offer less than its members hope for but may still be incentivizing for some who enroll in such membership.

title: Dense Subgraph Clustering and a New Cluster Ensemble Method
text:
Abstract
We propose DSC-Flow-Iter, a new community detection algorithm that is based on iterative extraction of dense subgraphs. Although DSC-Flow-Iter leaves many nodes unclustered, it is competitive with leading methods and has high-precision and low-recall, making it complementary to modularity-based methods that typically have high recall but lower precision. Based on this observation, we introduce a novel cluster ensemble technique that combines DSC-Flow-Iter with modularity-based clustering, to provide improved accuracy. We show that our proposed pipeline, which uses this ensemble technique, outperforms its individual components and improves upon the baseline techniques on a large collection of synthetic networks.

title: 2027 CG:SHOP: lawn mowing approximation
text:
Last week, we discussed the traveling salesman problem (TSP), which (as in lawn mowing) seeks the shortest tour to cover some object. The distinction is that TSP runs on a combinatorial object, while lawn mowing is a geometric problem on the plane. My goal today is to illustrate the thought process behind generalization, through an instructive case study in (Arkin et al. 2000). While the specific results are not the main point, they will also be used in future weeks.
See full notes.




References

Arkin, Esther M., Sándor P. Fekete, and Joseph S. B. Mitchell. 2000. “Approximation Algorithms for Lawn Mowing and Milling.” Computational Geometry 17 (1): 25–50. https://doi.org/https://doi.org/10.1016/S0925-7721(00)00015-8.

title: Unification
text:
Denote lowercase letters as unification variables. Denote uppercase letters among (F, P, L, N, S) as term constructors with arity 2, 2, 1, 0, 0 respectively.
We will run Unify { ('b = F(N, S)), (P('a, 'c) = P('c, 'b)) }, i.e. we have two constraints. The first asserts that the type variable 'b must be equal to F(N, S). The second asserts that the aggregate of two type variables P('a, 'c) must be equal to the aggregate P('c, 'b). The solution is obviously that

'a equals F(N, S)
'b equals F(N, S)
'c equals F(N, S)

Now, (one instantiation) of steps could be:

Unify { (P('a, 'c) = P('c, F(N, S))) } o {'b -> F(N, S)} by eliminate on 'b = F(N, S):
Unify { ('a = 'c), ('c = F(N, S)) } o {'b -> F(N, S)} by decompose on P('a, 'c) = P('c, F(N, S)):
Unify { ('a = F(N, S)) } o {'c = F(N, S)} o {'b -> F(N, S)} by eliminate on 'c = F(N, S):
Unify { } o {'a -> F(N, S)} o {'c = F(N, S)} o {'b -> F(N, S)} by eliminate on 'a = F(N, S):

And we get a final answer of: {'a -> F(N, S), 'b -> F(N, S), 'c -> F(N, S)}.

As another example, we will run Unify {(F('a,F('b,'b)) = F(P('c,L('c)), F(P('e,L('d)),P('c,'f)))), (P(P(N,'d),'c) = P('a,'c))}, i.e. now with 2 constraints that are more nested.

Unify {('a = P('c,L('c))), (F('b,'b) = F(P('e,L('d)),P('c,'f))), (P(P(N,'d),'c) = P('a,'c))} by Decompose on (F('a,F('b,'b)) = F(P('c,L('c)), F(P('e,L('d)),P('c,'f))))
Unify {('a = P('c,L('c))), (F('b,'b) = F(P('e,L('d)),P('c,'f))), (P(N,'d) = 'a), ('c = 'c)} by Decompose on (P(P(N,'d),'c) = P('a,'c))
Unify {('a = P('c,L('c))), (F('b,'b) = F(P('e,L('d)),P('c,'f))), (P(N,'d) = 'a)} by Delete on ('c = 'c)
Unify {('a = P('c,L('c))), (F('b,'b) = F(P('e,L('d)),P('c,'f))), ('a = P(N,'d))} by Orient on (P(N,'d) = 'a)
Unify {(P(N,'d) = P('c,L('c))), (F('b,'b) = F(P('e,L('d)),P('c,'f)))} o { 'a -> P(N, 'd) } by Eliminate on ('a = P(N,'d))
Unify {(N = 'c), ('d = L('c)), (F('b,'b) = F(P('e,L('d)),P('c,'f)))} o { 'a -> P(N, 'd) } by Decompose on (P(N,'d) = P('c,L('c)))
Unify {(N = 'c), (F('b,'b) = F(P('e,L(L('c))),P('c,'f)))} o {'d -> L('c)} o { 'a -> P(N, 'd) } by Eliminate on ('d = L('c))
Unify {('c = N), (F('b,'b) = F(P('e,L(L('c))),P('c,'f)))} o {'d -> L('c)} o { 'a -> P(N, 'd) } by Orient on (N = 'c)
Unify {(F('b,'b) = F(P('e,L(L(N))),P(N,'f)))} o {'c -> N} o {'d -> L('c)} o { 'a -> P(N, 'd) } by Eliminate on ('c = N)
Unify {('b = P('e,L(L(N)))), ('b = P(N,'f))} o {'c -> N} o {'d -> L('c)} o { 'a -> P(N, 'd) } by Decompose on (F('b,'b) = F(P('e,L(L(N))),P(N,'f)))
Unify {(P(N, 'f) = P('e,L(L(N))))} o {'c -> N} o {'b -> P(N, 'f)} o {'d -> L('c)} o { 'a -> P(N, 'd) } by Eliminate on ('b = P(N,'f))
Unify {(N = 'e), ('f = L(L(N)))} o {'c -> N} o {'b -> P(N, 'f)} o {'d -> L('c)} o { 'a -> P(N, 'd) } by Decompose on (P(N, 'f) = P('e,L(L(N))))
Unify {('e = N), ('f = L(L(N)))} o {'c -> N} o {'b -> P(N, 'f)} o {'d -> L('c)} o { 'a -> P(N, 'd) } by Orient on (N = 'e)
Unify {('f = L(L(N)))} o {'e -> N} o {'c -> N} o {'b -> P(N, 'f)} o {'d -> L('c)} o { 'a -> P(N, 'd) } by Eliminate on ('e = N)
Unify {} o {'f -> L(L(N))} o {'e -> N} o {'c -> N} o {'b -> P(N, 'f)} o {'d -> L('c)} o { 'a -> P(N, 'd) } by Eliminate on ('f = L(L(N)))

And we get a final answer of: {'f -> L(L(N)), 'e -> N, 'c -> N, 'b -> P(N, L(L(N))), 'd -> L(N), 'a -> P(N, L(N)) }

title: Type systems
text:
First, we specify a subset of the OCaml grammar subset. Associativity and precedence are not described here, and a description can be found in the Bison grammar picoml-stepper/interpreter/picoml.y.
This note will describe the static semantics of our language. In particular, each expression has a type \(\tau\) of possible data values. Our (sound) type system will a type for each expression, such that the dynamic value will always be in the type of \(\tau\).
Towards this, the main rule is the type judgment.
where \(\Gamma\) is our type environment (a context mapping variables to types), \(e\) is an expression, and \(\tau\) is some type. Then, under the type environemnt and a set of preconditions (above the bar), then we prove that \(e\) has type \(\tau\). A sound program has expressions for which the judgement \(\emptyset \vdash e : \tau\) is derivable. We will use \(\Gamma_1 + \Gamma_2\) to denote \(\Gamma_1 \cup (\Gamma_2 \setminus \Gamma_1)\) (note that this is not commutative).
Note that this is closely related to the idea of a logic system. Types correspond to propositions, and terms correspond to proofs. This is known as the Curry-Howard isomorphism; we will see that functions correspond to implication, and application corresponds to modus ponens.

title: Type systems
text:
A monomorphic type system
First, we give the rules for a very simple type system, in which each variable provably has a unique type. In contrast, a polymorphic type system can give a variable distinct types, as we will see later.
let x = fun y -> y + 2;;
Under our type system, we will assign \(x\) the type \(\textsf{int} \mapsto \textsf{int}\). Informally, if \(x\) is the type \(\textsf{int} \mapsto \textsf{int}\), then the binder \(y\) gets type \(\textsf{int}\), and the \(+\) operator will also return an integer. This is an example of a type derivation, and we will now provide judgements for proving the type of an expression (though we do not show soundness or completeness).
First, we can specify boolean constants




























































In the above rule, \(\Gamma\) is a meta-variable. Rather than writing a rule for every possible type environment, we write a schema in terms of \(\Gamma\). Note that the rules themselves are still in terms of the concrete syntax as before.
As another example of a meta-variable, say \(n\) is an integral constant, so that the rule says that \(1\) is an integer, \(2\) is an integer, and so on.
































Deriving the type of a variable involves looking in the type context.










































Another interesting example is to determine the type of a pair \((e_1, e_2)\). This rule has a precondition, that \(e_1: \tau_1\) and \(e_2: \tau_2\), and once these are set, then \((e_1, e_2)\) has type \(\tau_1 * \tau_2\).




























































So to derive the type of \((1, \texttt{false})\), then we have to first derive the type of both components \(1\) and \(\texttt{false}\). Indeed, it is typed is \(\textsf{int} * \textsf{bool}\).
(1, false)
and we can write a derivation for this as follows:




























































































Writing out the rules for the rest of our expression constructors is straightforward and intuitive.






















































































































































































































































































































































































































































































































































At this point, it is prudent to prove properties about the system we have thus given. One important property is that each \(x: \tau \in \Gamma\) has a unique \(\tau\). We will not prove it here, but intead illustrate these with a more in-depth example, showing (almost) all of our judgements.

Examples
let rec f x = if x <= 1 then 1 else x * f (x - 1) in f 3;;
We want to prove that this expression has type \(\textsf{int}\). We work backwards from the conclusion; our judgment rules are syntax driven and so there is only one possible rule to apply at each step.
First, the has two premises. The second is straightforward to derive: we first derive the types of both terms of the application \(f\) and \(3\) using the variable and constant rules respectively, before applying the application rule.



































































































































































































































































The other premise is a bit more involved. There are the function rules, and then the conditional, in which the three expressions have to be typed. The base case is trivial.















































































































































Let \(\Gamma_1 = \left\{ x: \textsf{int}, f: \textsf{int} \to \textsf{int} \right\}\).











































































































































As far as the predicate of the \(\textsf{if}\), we can indeed verify it types to a \(\textsf{bool}\).



































































































And as for the other side, we verify that it matches with the true branch of the if, namely that it also evaluates to an \(\textsf{int}\).

title: Type systems
text:
A polymorphic type system
The type system described above is very limited. Consider for example, the following expression:
let id x = x in (id 1, id false)
What type is \(\texttt{id}\)? For the first element of the pair, it seems like we need \(\texttt{id}: \textsf{int} \to \textsf{int}\), but for the second element, it seems like we need \(\texttt{id}: \textsf{bool} \to \textsf{bool}\). We need a more powerful type system to express the possibility for \(\texttt{id}\) to be both!
let id x = x
We see that OCaml gives \(\texttt{id}\) the type signature 'a -> 'a It is instructive to think of this as sugar for the universally quantified type \(\forall(\alpha . \alpha \to \alpha)\). We read this as the type is now a function taking a type as an argument, and in general denote as \(\forall(t . \tau)\).
In this system, beyond our basic and compound types in the monomorphic type system, we also introduce type variables (in OCaml, prefixed with a ', and in our mathematics, we use lowercase greek letters). Finally, every type has a universal quantifier dictating the bound variables.
In particular, consider the grammar for the types:






















































































































































Now, type judgements are still over monotypes






































But, as type environments are now mappings from variables to polytypes, they will hold more power. With this, we can consider the first judgment that must change: variables.

































































where \(\varphi\) is a function replacing each \(\alpha_i\) with a monotype. For example, if the type environment is \(\left\{ x: \alpha \right\}\), then \(x: \textsf{int}\) can be derived, and \(x: \textsf{bool}\) too.
The second judgment that must change is in assigning new variables in a let (i.e. modifying the type environment); we need to be able to create polytypes from monotypes. To do this, consider a new function
\[
    \mathbf{Gen}(\tau, \Gamma): \textsf{Monotype} \times \textsf{Environment} \to \textsf{Polytype}
\]
which will bind all the free variables in \(\tau\) that are not in \(\Gamma\). Namely, the free variables of monomorphic types are the type variables, of polymorphic types must remove the quantified vars, and for an environment, all free variables over the range.
Now, the modifications to the grammar are simple, with only the following rules changing.













































































































































































































































































Examples
To illustrate this, we shall consider three examples.
fun y -> let f = fun x -> y in (f 1, f true);;
We can derive the type as follows. In the second premise of LetIn, \(f\) is bound to \(\mathbf{Gen}(\beta \to \alpha, \left\{ y: \forall . \alpha \right\}) = \forall \beta . \beta \to \alpha\); only \(\beta\) is quantified, since \(\alpha\) is free in the environment.






































































































































































































































































































































































































































































































































































































































































Note that the derived type is \(\alpha * \alpha\); the output of \(f\) must be the same type even though it is a polytype. In contrast, consider the following, whose output pair type is \(\alpha * \beta\).
fun y -> let rec f = fun x -> f x in (f 1, f true);;
We can derive the type as follows.


























































































































































































Where in the first premise, the type environment is \(\Gamma_1 = \left\{ f: \forall . \delta \to \varepsilon, y: \forall . \alpha \right\}\).






















































































































and in the second premise, let \(\Gamma_2 = \left\{ f: \forall \delta, \varepsilon . \delta \to \varepsilon, y: \forall . \alpha \right\}\).





























































































































































And for the final example, we note that the following does not type check.
let rec f = fun x -> f (x, x);;
Indeed, we fail at the argument of the recursive call.















































































































































The type of \(f\) is not quantified inside its own body, so its input type is fixed to \(\alpha\). The premise \(\left\{ x: \forall . \alpha, f: \forall . \alpha \to \beta \right\} \vdash (x, x) : \alpha\) has no derivation: the pair rule only derives \((x, x) : \alpha * \alpha\), and no monotype \(\alpha\) is equal to \(\alpha * \alpha\).
The above is a case of our type system not allowing polymorphic recursion. However, OCaml does allow this when the types are explicitly written. Apparently, polymorphic recursion makes type inference undecidable.
let rec f: 'a . 'a -> int = fun x -> f (x, x);;
Indeed, this can be very powerful. Consider the following representation of a perfect binary tree, with values at the leaves.
type 'a perfect = Leaf of 'a | Node of ('a * 'a) perfect;;
We might want to find the depth for a perfect tree. A typical way might be to use mutual recursion for the two cases. However, it is more elegant to use the same depth function that is polymorphic, from a 'a perfect to ('a * 'a) perfect in the recursive call.
let rec depth : 'a . 'a perfect -> int =
fun t -> match t with
  | Leaf _ -> 0
  | Node t -> 1 + depth t in
let t = Node (Node (Leaf ((1, 2), (3, 4)))) in
    depth t;;
